title: The Son Called Angel and God: Jacob’s Ladder
english: … he who is before all things, and who governs every nature in a way beyond nature, should be none of all things, and should not be thought a creature by comparison with the things brought into being by him, which have received as their lot a complete difference from him.

Or to put it another way: if someone, attending to the truth and fully assured by the divine oracles, declares him the maker of everything that is made and the one who bears the whole creation, and names him the image of God and Son, how could he also confess him to be a thing made, or less than God who bears all things, or to have someone born before him, unless he were mad?

That he has been called both God and angel, the prophets foretell. Malachi says this: “The Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, the Lord is coming; and who will endure the day of his entrance? Or who will stand at his appearing?” (Malachi 3:1-2). The beginning of the saying shows the saving dispensation; what follows shows his second coming, fearful and full of love for mankind.

And Isaiah cries out, in the way people who share a joy are wont to announce it to those who have not yet learned what has happened: “A child has been born to us, a son also has been given, and his name is called Angel of great counsel, Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Potentate, Prince of peace” (Isaiah 9:6).

Jacob too calls this God the Word an angel, when, on his way to Mesopotamia, he fell asleep and saw a dream. For it says: “And behold, a ladder set firm on the earth, whose top reached to heaven; and the angels of God were going up and coming down on it. And the Lord stood firm upon it and said: I am the Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac. Do not fear. The land on which you are sleeping I will give to you and to your seed. And I will be with you and guard you on every way by which you go, and I will bring you back in safety to your father’s house. And your seed will spread out to the south and the west, to the north and the east” (Genesis 28:12-15).

Through the ladder the cross was foretold, by which the faithful go up to the heavenly dwellings; and the God who stood firm on the ladder is himself the one who of his own will was nailed to the cross for us.

And after other things: “Jacob vowed,” it says: “If the Lord God is with me and guards me on the way by which I go, and gives me bread to eat and a garment to put on, and brings me back in safety to my father’s house, then the Lord shall be my God; and this stone, which I have set up as a pillar, shall be to me a house of God; and of all that you give me I will give you a tenth” (Genesis 28:20-22).

Then, when he had prospered with Laban, at the time the flocks conceived (Genesis 31:10) he again saw in a vision the God who had appeared to him earlier, and he told it like this: “The angel of God said to me in my sleep: ‘Jacob, lift up your eyes and see the rams and the he-goats mounting the sheep and the she-goats; for I know all that Laban will do to you. I am the God who appeared to you on the way by which you were coming, where you set up a pillar to me and vowed a vow to me there’” (Genesis 31:11-13).

And in Egypt too the same Jacob asks this angel and “great God” for his blessing on the sons of Joseph, saying: “The God whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac pleased, the God who has fed me from my youth to this day, the angel who rescues me from all my evils” (Genesis 48:15-16).

On those who say that “the Father is incomparable and greater than the Son,” that “image is one thing and God another,” and that “man too was written to be the image and glory of God” (1 Corinthians 11:7); and on the testimony that the Father differs from the Son in nothing.

They assign incomparability and being greater to the Father because he is unbegotten, and unlikeness to the Son because he is begotten; once again they drag what concerns the most ineffable Godhead down to the conditions of our own nature and the …

added_allusions.reason: Didymus puts “great God” in quotation marks for the angel who blessed Joseph’s sons; the phrase is Paul’s title for Christ in Titus 2:13, not a word of Genesis 48
“the one who bears the whole creation” and “God who bears all things” echo “upholding all things by the word of his power”

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u04): retranslated from the Greek. The old draft broke Genesis 28:12-15 off mid-word ('upon l—') and resumed in the next paragraph, called the opening clause a 'That…' heading, made Jacob 'say' instead of vow, read κίσσησις (the flocks conceiving) as 'greenery of the pastures', turned the title's 'greater than the Son' into 'the Father of the Son is incomparable', and garbled 15.97-15.98, 15.99 and 15.107. 'Gen' references written in full; Genesis 31:10 and 1 Corinthians 11:7 added; bracket filler [possessions] removed. Ends mid-sentence as the Greek does.
